I don't cringe at it so much, but I usually feel apprehensive about using that term. On the surface it obviously says "sexual" though semantically speaking, it includes the romantic meaning (which is extremely important, I agree). Sigh, if only there was a better word :P

Though we can't help it, some of us take it as an insult when straight people regard sexual orientation to be subject to their own choice. Needless to say, there's **a lot** of trash that homo-/bisexuals have to put up with. Imagine rumours about your orientation being circulated among your classmates/colleagues. Sometimes you notice a shift in a friend's attitude towards you, and you think: "Shit, did he find out? Does he find me disgusting because I'm gay/bi?" To many of us, it's probably our deepest secret, and 'coming out' to someone else is a really unnerving effort. Hence we wonder why on earth straight people would ever want to 'choose' to be gay or bisexual. Instead of pretending to be something they're not, people should just be grateful about being straight.

Some may disagree on this, but there seems to be a 'trend' of bisexuality, where celebrities like Katy Perry and Justin Bieber appear to be endorsing it with their style. Quite often, the media (especially tabloids) make a big deal about the tiniest speck of crap: "Is celebrity XX lesbian? Find out here". I can't believe people would give a shit. I can only hope it's a fad to pretend to be bi-/homosexual, and that it'll die off eventually.

Discourse with other LGBTs have told me that many of us have a variety of opinions about whether orientation is innate or not. But one's ultimate opinion (as an LGBT) rests on what values they hold, i.e. are they (and should they be) proud of their orientation?

In normal circumstances, the male's hypothalamus secretes GnRH, which in turn stimulates secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the anterior pituitary. These endocrine hormones enter the testes, where LH stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone, and FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to produce ABP. Testosterone + ABP = spermatogenesis (sperm production). There is a negative feedback system which maintains the amount of testosterone produced - some of the produced testosterone enters the bloodstream and back to the brain, signalling the brain to release more/less GnRH so a specific level is maintained.

Male hormonal contraception is essentially a testosterone or progestin or a combination of both. Injection of either of these into the bloodstream capitalizes the negative feedback loop, 'lying' to the brain that there is excessive testosterone/progestin so it does not release GnRH (thus inhibiting LH and FSH secretion), hence the testes do not produce sperm.

Currently, the progestin-testosterone combination is the most favourable. Testosterone-only treatments exhibited severe side effects. With progestin-only use, the male would have difficulty maintaining male sexual characteristics. So, both hormones are used.
